context.full_target:
Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
context.conclusion: dim_H(F)=D+1, where F=E×[0,1] has the Euclidean product metric and D=dim_H(E); equivalently dim_H(E×[0,1])=dim_H(E)+1 in ℝ^{n+1}.

record.type: family of Euclidean metric spaces indexed by natural numbers, together with their coordinate notation
record.definition: For each natural k, V(k)=ℝ^k, the functions from {0,...,k-1} to ℝ, with distance d(x,y)=(Σ_{j=0}^{k-1}(x_j-y_j)^2)^(1/2) and its metric topology and Borel measurable structure. V(0) consists of the single empty tuple. ℝ has its usual absolute-value distance. V(k)×ℝ always means the metric with squared distance d(x,y)^2+|t-u|^2, not the max-product metric. Concatenation (x,t)↦(x_0,...,x_{k-1},t) specifies the identification with V(k+1).

record.type: extended nonnegative diameter of a subset of a metric or extended metric space
record.definition: For an extended metric space X and A⊆X, diam(A)=sup{edist(x,y):x∈A,y∈A} in [0,∞], with supremum of the empty set equal to 0. On a metric space edist is ordinary distance viewed in [0,∞]. This is the native Metric.ediam. When diam(A) is bounded by a finite scale we identify it with its finite nonnegative real value. In particular empty sets and singletons have diameter zero.

record.type: positive-exponent unnormalized Hausdorff contents and measure, valued in [0,∞]
record.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero.

binders.type: countable family of subsets of that Euclidean space

record.type: native Hausdorff measures on Borel extended metric spaces, indexed by real exponents
record.definition: μH[d] on a Borel extended metric space X denotes MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure d, defined natively as Measure.mkMetric(r↦r^d), the metric outer-measure construction with diameter gauge r^d followed by its Borel measure. The metric outer construction is the supremum over positive extended scales r of the infimum of Σ_i (sup_{h:U_i≠∅} diam(U_i)^d) over sequences U:ℕ→Set X covering the set and satisfying diam(U_i)≤r. Empty summands are zero, including at exponent zero. Native ENNReal real powers are used. The value formula for the resulting measure on arbitrary subsets is established by the registered native theorem; its identification with H for positive exponents is proved below.

binders.type: extended metric space with its Borel measurable structure

record.type: Hausdorff dimension of a subset of a metric space, valued in [0,∞]
record.definition: For a subset A of a metric space with its Borel structure, dim_H(A)=sup{u:u∈[0,∞) is finite and μH[u](A)=∞}, with supremum of the empty set zero. The metric space may be borelized when no measurable structure was specified. This is the native dimH definition. Thus dim_H(∅)=0 by this convention. In this task it is applied to Euclidean subsets and the Euclidean product metric of V(n)×ℝ.

record.type: subset of V(n)×ℝ with the Euclidean product metric
record.definition: F=E×I={(x,t):x∈E,t∈I}, using the squared-distance product metric specified in V. Its Euclidean identification is the concatenation map to V(n+1).
D=dim_H(E). When finiteness is proved, finite dimensions are also viewed as nonnegative real numbers through the canonical inclusion ℝ≥0→[0,∞].

record.type: predicate on subsets of metric spaces
record.definition: Compact(A) means that every family of open sets whose union contains A has a finite subfamily whose union contains A. The word compact has this finite-open-subcover meaning throughout.

record.type: Lebesgue measure on the Borel real line, also evaluated as outer measure on arbitrary sets
record.definition: λ is the native MeasureTheory.volume on ℝ, equivalently the Lebesgue measure whose outer measure is the infimum of sums of lengths of countable open-interval covers. As for any measure, λ is monotone, has λ(∅)=0, and is countably additive on disjoint measurable sets. These measure axioms are part of the measure structure, not any assertion of measurability of the arbitrary covering sets in this proof.

record.type: nonnegative Lebesgue integral for an arbitrary measure on a measurable space
record.definition: For a measurable space X, a measure ν on it, and f:X→[0,∞], LInt(ν,f)=∫⁻ f dν is the supremum of the simple-function integrals Σ_a a ν(g^{-1}{a}) over nonnegative measurable finite-range simple functions g≤f, with 0·∞=0. This is the native MeasureTheory.lintegral. For measurable f the value may be ∞; no finite-integrability premise is implicit.

record.type: indicator operation for nonnegative functions on a set
record.definition: For B⊆X and c∈[0,∞], ind(B,c)(t)=c if t∈B and 0 otherwise. It denotes native Set.indicator B (fun _=>c). Thus c·1_B is an alternative notation for ind(B,c).

record.statement: For every Euclidean subset A and s>0, the supplied unnormalized H^s(A) equals native μH[s](A). The native dim_H therefore has the following critical-exponent properties with this H: s>dim_H(A) implies H^s(A)=0; 0<s<dim_H(A) implies H^s(A)=∞; H^s(A)=0 implies dim_H(A)≤s; H^s(A)=∞ implies dim_H(A)≥s. Always dim_H(A)≥0. For 0<δ≤r, H^s_δ(A)≥H^s_r(A), and H^s(A)=sup_{δ>0}H^s_δ(A); if H^s(A)=∞ these contents are unbounded as δ↓0. If A⊆B in one Euclidean space, then dim_H(A)≤dim_H(B). If φ:A→Y is distance preserving into another Euclidean space Y, then H^s(φ(A))=H^s(A) for every s>0 and dim_H(φ(A))=dim_H(A), with both sets given their ambient Euclidean metrics. For every a>0, h^a→0 as h↓0; for every b<0, h^b→∞ as h↓0. Nonnegative series are sums in [0,∞], i.e. suprema of finite partial sums; Σ_{i≥0}2^{-i-1}=1 and Σ_{i≥0}2^{-i-2}=1/2.
